about: The starter drill library for Clean Sheet.
Every entry here is written from scratch in our own words. Nothing is copied from
The FA's England Football Learning site, the FIFA Training Centre, or anywhere else.
Where a drill overlaps with a published FA or FIFA resource we link out to it as
further reading in `references` — we never reproduce their text, images or video.
See docs/content-policy.md before adding anything to this file.
References deliberately point at section landing pages rather than deep article
URLs, which rot quickly and would send coaches to a 404 mid-session.

drills.name: Traffic Lights
drills.summary: Ball-mastery warm-up where colours tell players to stop, go, or turn.
drills.description:
Every player has a ball inside the grid and dribbles freely. The coach calls a colour and the players react: **green** is dribble at speed into space, **amber** is slow it down with lots of small touches, **red** is stop the ball dead with the sole of the foot.

It gets a whole squad moving with a ball each inside thirty seconds, which is exactly what you want on a cold Tuesday when players are arriving in dribs and drabs. Add and remove players without stopping the activity.
drills.setup: A 20x20 yard grid marked with cones. One ball per player. Adjust the grid so it feels slightly crowded — players should have to lift their heads to avoid each other.
coachingPoints: Head up between touches — can you see the space before you move into it?
Use the sole of the foot to stop the ball cleanly on 'red'
Little touches when you're near someone, bigger touches when you're in space
Use both feet — try the next 'red' with your other foot
progressions: Add a colour for a turn (e.g. 'blue' = drag-back and go the other way)
Call two colours in a row so players have to hold a sequence in their head
Shrink the grid to increase the number of near-misses
regressions: Use just green and red until the group is confident
Make the grid bigger so there is less traffic to deal with

references.label: England Football Learning — coaching the youngest age groups

diagram.caption: Everyone has a ball; the coach calls a colour.

drills.name: Passing Gates
drills.summary: Pairs score a point every time they pass cleanly through any gate.
drills.description:
Scatter small cone gates around the area. In pairs with one ball, players move around and pass to each other through any gate they can find. A pass counts only if the ball goes through a gate and the partner controls it on the other side.

The scoring is what makes it work — pairs start hunting for gates rather than standing still, so you get movement, scanning and passing without ever telling anyone to move.
drills.setup: A 25x25 yard area with 8-10 gates made from pairs of cones, roughly 2 yards wide, scattered at all angles. One ball between two.
coachingPoints: Look for the gate before you receive, not after
Pass firmly — a soft pass through a gate is easy to intercept in a real game
Move to a new angle straight after you pass
Talk to your partner: tell them which gate you're heading for
progressions: Count as a pair and ask them to beat their own score in the next 90 seconds
No repeating the same gate twice in a row
Add two defenders who intercept and win the ball for their own count
regressions: Make the gates wider
Let the receiving player use as many touches as they need

references.label: England Football Learning — practice design and session planning

diagram.caption: Pairs score a point for every clean pass through any gate.

drills.name: Sharks and Minnows
drills.summary: Dribble across the area without losing your ball to the sharks.
drills.description:
The minnows line up on one side with a ball each. One or two sharks start in the middle with no ball. On the call, the minnows dribble to the far side. Sharks try to kick the balls out of the area.

A minnow who loses their ball becomes a shark, so the game gets harder as it goes and the last player standing has earned it. Everyone is involved the whole time — nobody is queuing.
drills.setup: A 20x25 yard area. One ball per minnow. Start with one shark for every eight players.
coachingPoints: Keep the ball close when a shark is near, push it further when the path is clear
Look up and pick the gap before you set off
Use your body between the shark and the ball
Change direction rather than running into trouble
progressions: Sharks must dribble the won ball out rather than just kicking it away
Narrow the area so there is less space to escape into
regressions: Widen the area
Sharks can only move sideways along the middle line
A player who loses the ball can retrieve it and rejoin as a minnow

diagram.caption: Minnows dribble across; sharks try to win the balls.

drills.name: Pass and Follow Triangle
drills.summary: Continuous passing round a triangle where you always follow your pass.
drills.description:
Three cones form a triangle with players split between them. Player passes to the next cone, then jogs to join the back of the queue they just passed to. The ball moves round the triangle continuously.

It looks simple, and it is — that is the point of a warm-up. What it does buy you is a lot of repetitions of a clean pass and a first touch out of the feet, plus a chance to see who is comfortable on their weaker side.
drills.setup: Three cones in a triangle roughly 8-10 yards apart. Two to four players at each cone. One ball per triangle; add a second ball once it is flowing.
coachingPoints: First touch out of your feet and into the direction you're passing
Pass along the ground with the inside of the foot
Call the name of the player you're passing to
Follow your pass at a jog, not a walk
progressions: Add a second ball going the other way round
Two touches maximum, then one
Receive with the back foot and open your body before passing
regressions: Shorten the distance between cones
Unlimited touches while players find their rhythm

diagram.caption: Pass, then follow your pass to the next cone.

drills.name: Ball Mastery Grid
drills.summary: Individual ball work: sole rolls, toe taps, drag-backs and turns.
drills.description:
Each player has a ball in their own small square. The coach demonstrates a move, players copy it for 45 seconds, then everyone dribbles to a new square before the next move.

Rotate through: sole rolls side to side, toe taps on top of the ball, drag-back turns, inside-outside touches, and the Cruyff turn. The moving-square bit matters — it keeps it feeling like a game rather than a drill, and it gets heads up between reps.
drills.setup: A grid of small 3x3 yard squares, one per player, marked with four cones each (or one cone if you're short). One ball per player.
coachingPoints: Quality over speed — get it right slowly first
Both feet, every time
Head up for a moment between each repetition
Stay on your toes, not flat-footed
progressions: Speed it up and count repetitions in 30 seconds
Players invent a move and teach it to the group
Perform the move then accelerate out of the square for three touches
regressions: Fewer moves, more time on each
Demonstrate alongside a player who has it, so there are two models to watch

references.label: FIFA Training Centre — grassroots coaching resources

diagram.caption: One small square each; move to a new one between moves.

drills.name: Rondo 4v1
drills.summary: Four players keep the ball in a square while one defender tries to win it.
drills.description:
Four attackers stand around the edges of a square, one defender inside. The attackers keep the ball away from the defender. If the defender wins it or forces it out, the player responsible goes in.

The rondo is the most efficient possession practice there is — high touches, constant decisions, and the defender never gets a rest. Keep the groups small so nobody is waiting.
drills.setup: A 10x10 yard square per group of five. Attackers stay on the edges; the defender works inside. One ball per square.
coachingPoints: Open your body before the ball arrives so you can see both ways out
Play the pass you can see, not the one you want to see
Move along your edge to open a passing line
Defender: close the nearest passing lane rather than chasing the ball
progressions: Two touches maximum, then one touch
Add a second defender to make it 4v2
A pass split between the two defenders counts double
regressions: Make the square bigger
Allow unlimited touches
Defender starts passive, only closing down at walking pace

references.label: England Football Learning — possession and playing out

diagram.caption: Four on the edges, one defender inside.

drills.name: Third-Man Runs in a Diamond
drills.summary: Practise the pass that sets up the pass — receiving from a player you didn't pass to.
drills.description:
Four players in a diamond. The player at the base passes to a side player, who sets it back or sideways, and the ball is then played on to the player at the top — who was moving before the ball came. The receiver at the top is the 'third man': they get the ball from a pass they were never part of.

This is one of the harder ideas to teach and one of the most valuable. Start slow and unopposed. The moment they see it work in a game it clicks.
drills.setup: A diamond of four cones roughly 10 yards apart. Four players per diamond, one ball. Rotate one position clockwise every two minutes.
coachingPoints: Third man: start your run before the second pass is played
Set the ball back with a firm, accurate touch — a bobbling set-back kills the move
Scan over your shoulder before you receive
Time the run so you arrive as the ball does, not before
progressions: Add a passive defender in the middle
Limit to two touches throughout
Finish the sequence with a shot or a pass into a target goal
regressions: Walk through the pattern with no ball first
Let the third man stand still and receive to feet

references.label: England Football Learning — attacking principles and combination play

diagram.caption: Base to side, set, then in behind to the third man.

drills.name: Two-Touch Passing Squares
drills.summary: Four players, one square, one ball — control and pass, endlessly.
drills.description:
Players stand on the four corners of a square. The ball goes round the square with two touches: one to control, one to pass. After ten clean circuits, change direction. After twenty, switch to diagonal passes across the square.

Unfussy and repetitive on purpose. Use it when the group needs to settle down and get some quality touches in before something more demanding.
drills.setup: A 12x12 yard square, one player per corner, one ball. Multiple squares run in parallel.
coachingPoints: First touch away from your body, into space
Second touch is the pass — no dawdling
Weight the pass so it arrives at a comfortable pace
Point at where you want the ball before it comes
progressions: One touch only
Follow your pass and swap corners
Add a second ball travelling the opposite way
regressions: Three touches allowed
Shrink the square so passes are shorter

diagram.caption: One touch to control, one to pass, round the square.

drills.name: First Touch Turn Gates
drills.summary: Receive with your back to the pitch, turn, and dribble through a gate.
drills.description:
A server plays a firm pass into a player standing with their back to the gates. The receiver takes one touch to turn out of the pass, then dribbles through any gate behind them. Then they become the server.

The skill being trained is the turn — the touch that takes you from facing the wrong way to facing the right way in a single movement. Encourage them to try different turns rather than always using the same one.
drills.setup: Servers on one line, receivers 8 yards away with their backs to three gates set 10 yards behind them. One ball per pair.
coachingPoints: Check over your shoulder before the ball arrives — which gate is free?
Open your hips as the ball comes so the first touch takes you round
Touch the ball into space, not under your feet
Accelerate away after the turn
progressions: Add a defender pressing from behind
Server calls the gate number as they pass
Two-touch limit: turn and go
regressions: Softer, slower service
Allow a controlling touch before the turning touch

diagram.caption: Receive with your back to the gates, turn, and go through one.

drills.name: 1v1 Gate Duels
drills.summary: Attacker tries to dribble through any of three gates; defender tries to stop them.
drills.description:
One attacker with a ball starts 10 yards from a defender. Behind the defender are three gates. The attacker scores by dribbling through any gate under control. The defender scores by winning the ball or forcing it out.

Three gates rather than one is the whole trick: the defender cannot simply stand in the way, so the attacker has to look up, pick a side, and commit. Swap roles every turn so everyone gets both jobs.
drills.setup: A 15x12 yard channel. Three gates spread across the end line, each 2 yards wide. Attackers queue at one end with a ball each.
coachingPoints: Attacker: run at the defender with the ball, not away from it — make them decide
Change of pace beats change of direction on its own
Defender: side-on stance, show them to one side, don't dive in
Defender: stay on your toes and close the space slowly
progressions: Reduce to two gates so decisions come faster
Defender starts closer, giving the attacker less time
Winner stays on and faces the next player
regressions: Widen the gates
Defender starts passive and only becomes live after the attacker's second touch

references.label: England Football Learning — 1v1 and individual possession

diagram.caption: Three gates to attack — the defender cannot cover them all.

drills.name: Beat the Defender Channels
drills.summary: Repeated 1v1s in narrow channels, so nobody hides and nobody queues.
drills.description:
Split the pitch into three or four narrow channels running end to end. Each channel has an attacker and a defender working continuously: attacker tries to reach the far line under control, then turns and goes back the other way against the same defender. Swap after 90 seconds.

The narrow channel forces a genuine 1v1 — there's nowhere to run around the problem. Short, sharp bursts with real rest in between.
drills.setup: Channels roughly 8 yards wide by 20 yards long, marked with cones. One ball per channel, two players per channel.
coachingPoints: Attacker: get the defender moving before you commit to a direction
Protect the ball with your body when the defender gets close
Defender: don't let them turn you — stay goal-side and patient
Defender: force them onto their weaker foot
progressions: Narrow the channel further
Add a time limit — 8 seconds to get to the far line
Winner of each duel moves up a channel, loser moves down
regressions: Widen the channel
Defender may only tackle inside the final five yards

diagram.caption: Narrow channels — nowhere to run around the problem.

drills.name: Shooting Ladder
drills.summary: Three shooting stations at increasing distance, run as a rotation.
drills.description:
Set three shooting positions: close range inside the box, edge of the box, and just outside. Players work round all three, one shot at each, then collect their ball and rejoin.

The point of the ladder is that the technique has to change with the distance — a side-foot finish close in, a firmer laces strike further out. Ask them what changed rather than telling them.
drills.setup: A goal with a keeper (or a target goal if you have none). Three cone positions at roughly 6, 14 and 20 yards. A supply of balls beside each position.
coachingPoints: Look at the goal before you look at the ball
Close range: side foot, accuracy over power, pick your corner
Longer range: laces, non-kicking foot alongside the ball, follow through
Head still and over the ball to keep the shot down
progressions: Add a pass in before the shot, so it's a moving ball
One-touch finishes only at the close station
Add a recovering defender chasing from behind
regressions: Move every station closer
Stationary ball, unlimited time

diagram.caption: Three stations — the technique changes with the distance.

drills.name: Cross and Finish Waves
drills.summary: Wide player delivers, two attackers arrive at the near and far post.
drills.description:
A wide player dribbles to the by-line and crosses. Two attackers start centrally and time their runs — one to the near post, one to the far. Alternate the side the cross comes from so both feet get used.

At younger ages the crossing itself is hard, so lower the expectation on the delivery and coach the runs. A cut-back along the ground counts as a cross and is often the better ball anyway.
drills.setup: Half a pitch with a goal and a keeper. Wide starting cones on both flanks, a queue of attackers in the centre circle. Plenty of balls with the wide players.
coachingPoints: Near-post runner: attack the ball, get in front of your defender
Far-post runner: stay wide and behind, arrive late
Crosser: head up before you deliver — where are they?
A cut-back along the ground is often better than a high cross
progressions: Add one or two defenders in the box
Add a third runner arriving at the edge of the area for the cut-back
First-time finishes only
regressions: Crosser can carry the ball to a set position and deliver unopposed with time
Attackers walk their runs through first with no ball

diagram.caption: Near-post and far-post runs, timed to the delivery.

drills.name: Press the Cone
drills.summary: Teach the approach: closing down under control rather than sprinting in.
drills.description:
A defender starts 10 yards from a cone with a ball on it. On the call they close the ball down, arriving side-on with short steps in the final two yards, and touch the ball with the sole of the foot without knocking the cone over.

Stripping out the attacker for a few minutes lets you actually coach the approach — which is the part most young defenders get wrong. Then put an attacker back in and see if it holds up.
drills.setup: Cones spread out with a ball resting beside each. Defenders in pairs, one working, one watching and giving feedback.
coachingPoints: Fast for the first two-thirds, slow for the last third
Arrive side-on, not square — show them one way
Small steps at the end so you can react either way
Stay on your toes with a low centre of gravity
progressions: Replace the cone with a live attacker who may go either way
Two defenders press together, one pressing and one covering
Add a time limit on the approach
regressions: Walk the approach through in slow motion
Shorten the starting distance

diagram.caption: Fast for two-thirds, slow and side-on for the last third.

drills.name: Goalkeeper Handling Circuit
drills.summary: Three stations of handling work — low, mid-height and diving.
drills.description:
Three short stations for your keeper (or keepers) to rotate through: rolled balls to gather low, waist-height balls into a secure chest catch, and balls thrown wide to dive and hold.

Most grassroots keepers get no specific work at all, so ten focused minutes goes a long way. If you only have one keeper, pair them with an outfield player who fancies a go — it usually reveals someone.
drills.setup: One goal or a marked 5-yard area. A server with a supply of balls at each station. Cones marking the working area.
coachingPoints: Hands behind the ball, fingers spread, thumbs together for high balls
Get your body behind the line of the ball wherever possible
Low balls: get down early, don't reach with hands alone
Hold it if you can, push it wide of the post if you can't
progressions: Serve without announcing the height
Add a shot from a moving ball
Keeper distributes accurately to a target after each save
regressions: Slow underarm serves, straight at the keeper
Kneeling starts for the diving station so there is less to think about

diagram.caption: Low, mid-height, then diving — rotate through.

drills.name: Y-Drill Combination
drills.summary: Pass, set, spin — a repeatable three-player combination ending in a shot.
drills.description:
A midfielder passes into a striker who has come short. The striker sets it first-time to a supporting player, who plays it into the path of the midfielder spinning off into the space behind. Finish with a shot.

Unopposed to begin with, so the pattern lands. It is the same idea as the third-man run but with a goal at the end, which tends to hold attention better.
drills.setup: A Y shape of cones on the edge of the final third, with a goal. Three players per repetition, plus a keeper. Rotate positions after each go.
coachingPoints: Striker: come towards the ball, don't wait for it
The set-back must be first time and firm
Spin off the shoulder as the set is played, not before
Take the shot early — the space closes fast
progressions: Add a defender marking the striker
One touch throughout the combination
Alternate sides so both feet are used
regressions: Walk the pattern with no defenders and no time pressure
Allow two touches on the set-back

diagram.caption: Pass in, set back, spin off into the space behind.

drills.name: 4v4 Four-Goal Game
drills.summary: Two teams, four mini goals — attack whichever one is unguarded.
drills.description:
Two teams of four play in a square with two small goals to attack on opposite sides. Because there are two goals to defend, teams get pulled apart and space appears constantly.

This is the small-sided game we come back to most. Everyone touches the ball, the picture changes every few seconds, and switching play stops being an abstract instruction and becomes the obvious thing to do.
drills.setup: A 30x25 yard area. Two mini goals (or cone goals) on each end line, set wide apart. Bibs for one team. One ball, with spares around the edge to keep it flowing.
coachingPoints: Which goal is less protected? Attack that one
Switch the ball quickly when one side gets crowded
Spread out when you have the ball, squeeze together when you don't
First defender presses, everyone else slides across
progressions: Must score in a different goal from the last one
Three-touch maximum
Add a neutral player who always plays for the team in possession
regressions: Bigger area, fewer players
Widen the goals
Remove touch limits entirely

references.label: England Football Learning — small-sided games and youth formats
FIFA Training Centre — grassroots small-sided football

diagram.caption: Two goals each to attack — the pitch keeps stretching.

drills.name: 3v3 End Zone Game
drills.summary: Score by dribbling or passing into the end zone and controlling the ball there.
drills.description:
Two teams of three. Instead of goals, each team attacks an end zone: a point is scored when a player controls the ball inside the opposition zone, having received it there or dribbled in.

Taking the goals away shifts the focus onto getting the ball forward and supporting the player who has it. It also means no keeper, so all six players are in the game.
drills.setup: A 25x20 yard area with 3-yard end zones marked at each end. Bibs for one team. One ball.
coachingPoints: Support in front of and behind the ball, not alongside
Can you play forward? If not, keep it and wait
Time your run into the end zone — don't camp in it
Defenders: protect the zone first, press the ball second
progressions: Ball must be passed into the zone, not dribbled
Two-touch limit
Play 3v3 plus a floating neutral
regressions: Deeper end zones
Larger area
Allow a player to stand permanently in the end zone as a target

diagram.caption: Control the ball in the end zone to score.

drills.name: 2v2 Continuous Duels
drills.summary: Rolling 2v2s to goal — win it, attack it, and the next pair comes straight on.
drills.description:
Two attackers take on two defenders towards a goal with a keeper. As soon as the ball goes dead, the coach serves a new ball to the next waiting pair from the opposite side, and the previous defenders become the new attackers.

Continuous means nobody stands still and the transition moment — the second the ball changes hands — happens over and over, which is exactly the moment most goals come from.
drills.setup: Half a pitch, one goal with a keeper. Two queues of pairs on either side of the halfway line. A big supply of balls with the coach.
coachingPoints: Attackers: one goes, one supports — never both in the same space
Attack the goal quickly before the defenders are set
Defenders: one presses, one covers behind
React the instant the ball turns over — first two seconds decide it
progressions: Serve to the defenders sometimes, so they must counter-attack
10-second time limit to score
Make it 3v2 to create an overload
regressions: Longer gaps between serves so players can reset
Play 2v1 in the attackers' favour

diagram.caption: Ball goes dead, next pair comes straight on.

drills.name: Overload 4v2 to Goal
drills.summary: Four attackers against two defenders — use the extra players properly.
drills.description:
Four attackers try to score against two defenders and a keeper. If the defenders win the ball, they score by dribbling over the halfway line.

The overload is deliberate: with a two-player advantage there is almost always a free player, and the coaching is about finding them rather than forcing it. Give the defenders a real way to score or they stop trying.
drills.setup: Half a pitch, goal and keeper at one end, halfway line as the defenders' target. Bibs for the defenders. Rotate roles every three minutes.
coachingPoints: Find the free player — there is always one
Move the defenders with the ball before you commit
Width first, then attack the space it creates
Defenders: stay compact and delay; don't both go to the ball
progressions: Reduce to 4v3
Two-touch limit for the attackers
Attackers must score within 15 seconds
regressions: Make it 5v2
Defenders start passive for the first three passes

diagram.caption: Two spare players — the coaching is finding them.

drills.name: 5v5 Two-Touch Game
drills.summary: A normal small-sided game with a two-touch limit to speed up the thinking.
drills.description:
A standard 5v5 with goals and keepers, but nobody may take more than two touches. The restriction forces players to decide where the ball is going before it arrives.

Use it as a follow-on once a passing theme has been introduced. Expect it to be scrappy for the first three minutes — let them work through that rather than stopping it.
drills.setup: A 40x30 yard pitch with a goal at each end. Bibs for one team. Spare balls behind each goal.
coachingPoints: Decide before the ball arrives — scan early and often
First touch sets up the second, so make it count
Off the ball: give them an easy option, quickly
Angles, not straight lines — make yourself passable to
progressions: One touch only for two minutes
A goal scored first-time counts double
regressions: Three touches
Remove the limit in your own half only
Bigger pitch to buy more time

diagram.caption: Two touches maximum — decide before it arrives.

drills.name: Score in Any Goal
drills.summary: Four goals scattered around the area, both teams can score in any of them.
drills.description:
Set four mini goals at random points inside the playing area rather than on the lines. Both teams may score in any goal, from either side. Defenders have to think about four targets at once, so they can never be fully organised.

Chaotic in the best way. Brilliant for younger groups and for the end of a session when concentration is fading but energy isn't.
drills.setup: A 30x30 yard area with four mini goals (or cone goals) placed inside it, well away from the edges. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Head up — which goal has nobody near it?
Change direction quickly when a goal gets covered
Look for the goal behind the defence, not just in front of you
Defend the ball and the nearest goal at the same time
progressions: Must use a different goal each time
Only score with a first-time finish
regressions: Fewer players in the same area
Widen the goals

diagram.caption: Four goals inside the area — look for the empty one.

drills.name: Playing Out From the Back 6v4
drills.summary: Build from the keeper against a pressing forward line and beat the first press.
drills.description:
A keeper plus a back four and a midfielder try to play out of their own third against four pressing attackers. The defending team succeeds by getting the ball under control past a line of cones at the halfway point. The attackers score in the goal if they win it.

The realistic bit is the pressure — if the attackers aren't genuinely trying, nobody learns anything. Give them a real incentive to win it back.
drills.setup: One third of a pitch, a full goal and keeper at one end, a line of cones marking the target line. Bibs for the pressing team.
coachingPoints: Get wide and deep early to stretch the press
The keeper is a player — use them to switch the ball
Play through the press when you can, over it when you can't
If the first option isn't on, go back and around — don't force it
progressions: Add a fifth presser
Two-touch limit for the defending team
Attackers must press within three seconds of the ball being played
regressions: Fewer pressers, making it 6v3
Pressers may not enter the penalty area
Walk it through unopposed once first

references.label: England Football Learning — playing out from the back

diagram.caption: Beat the press and get the ball over the line under control.

drills.name: Defending the Middle Third
drills.summary: A back four and two midfielders defend as a unit against an attacking six.
drills.description:
Six attackers try to get through the middle third and score. Six defenders work as a unit to stop them, scoring themselves by winning it and playing into either of two wide target zones.

The focus is the shape between the players rather than the individual tackle. Freeze it occasionally and ask the defenders where they'd be if the ball were five yards further left.
drills.setup: The middle third of a pitch plus a goal at one end. Two wide target zones behind the defending team's starting position. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Press the ball, everyone else shifts across together
Stay compact — no gaps between the lines for them to play into
Show them wide, away from the middle
Communicate: someone tells the unit when to step up
progressions: Give the attackers a time limit to break through
Add a seventh attacker to create an overload
Defenders must make three passes after winning it
regressions: Reduce the attackers to five
Narrow the playing area
Walk the shifting shape through slowly with the ball being moved by hand

references.label: England Football Learning — defending as a team

diagram.caption: Press the ball, everyone else shifts across together.

drills.name: Attacking Wide Areas 7v5
drills.summary: Attack with an overload and use the width to create a chance.
drills.description:
Seven attackers play against five defenders and a keeper in the attacking half. Wide channels are marked, and a goal scored from a cross or cut-back originating in a channel counts double.

The double-points rule does the coaching for you — players start looking for the wide player without being told. Rotate the defending group often; it's hard work.
drills.setup: Half a pitch, one goal with a keeper. Wide channels 6 yards deep marked down both flanks. Bibs for the defenders.
coachingPoints: Get the ball wide early, before the defence is set
Someone must attack the near post every single time
Cut-backs beat high crosses more often than you'd think
Overlap or underlap — give the wide player a decision to make
progressions: Reduce to 6v5
Limit the attack to 20 seconds
Defenders counter into a target goal on halfway
regressions: Only one defender allowed in each wide channel
Make it 8v4

diagram.caption: A goal from a wide delivery counts double.

drills.name: Conditioned Match: Three Passes
drills.summary: A normal match, but a team must string three passes together before scoring.
drills.description:
Play a regular match with one condition: three consecutive passes by the attacking team before a goal counts. It rewards the group that keeps the ball rather than the one that hoofs it and chases.

Drop the condition for the last five minutes and just let them play. That final stretch of free football is the bit most of them came for, and it's worth protecting.
drills.setup: The largest pitch and biggest goals you have. Even teams, bibs for one side. Spare balls all round the outside so restarts are quick.
coachingPoints: Count the passes out loud as a team
Keep the pitch big when you have it, small when you don't
Look forward first — the condition isn't an excuse to go sideways
Support the player on the ball quickly
progressions: Increase to five passes
Passes must include a switch from one side to the other
regressions: Two passes
Remove the condition and play freely

diagram.caption: Three consecutive passes before a goal counts.

drills.name: Free Play Match
drills.summary: Let them play. Coach with questions, not instructions.
drills.description:
A straight match with no conditions. The coach stays quiet for long stretches and, when the ball goes out, asks a question rather than giving an answer: *what did you see there?*, *what else could you have done?*, *what would you try next time?*

This is the hardest thing on the list to do well, because the instinct is to shout. Resist it. The players' own answers stick far better than anything shouted from the touchline.
drills.setup: The biggest pitch you can mark out, proper goals if you have them. Even teams. Bibs. Spare balls around the edges.
coachingPoints: Ask, don't tell — one question per stoppage at most
Let mistakes play out; the game is the teacher
Praise the attempt, not just the outcome
Rotate positions so nobody gets stuck in one role every week
progressions: Rotate positions every five minutes
Give each player one individual challenge to work on
regressions: Smaller pitch and fewer players so everyone gets more touches
Play in two separate smaller games rather than one big one

references.label: FIFA Training Centre — grassroots coaching philosophy

drills.name: Cool-Down Circle
drills.summary: Gentle movement, then two questions that make the session stick.
drills.description:
Bring everyone into a circle. Two minutes of easy movement and stretching while you talk, then ask two questions: *what's one thing you did well tonight?* and *what's one thing you'll try next week?*

Going round the circle means every player says something out loud, including the quiet ones. It takes three minutes and it is the part players most often repeat to their parents in the car.
drills.setup: A circle in the middle of the pitch. No equipment needed. Balls collected and bagged first so nobody is fiddling with one.
coachingPoints: Every player speaks — go round the circle, don't take volunteers
Accept every answer without correcting it
Name one specific thing you saw from each player if you can
Finish on time; parents are waiting and it builds trust
progressions: Players nominate a teammate for something they did well
Set an individual challenge for the week ahead
regressions: One question instead of two
Thumbs up or down instead of speaking, for shy groups

references.label: England Football Learning — reflection and player development

diagram.caption: Everyone speaks — go round the circle rather than taking hands up.

drills.name: Juggling Challenge Cool-Down
drills.summary: Low-intensity individual and partner juggling to wind down.
drills.description:
Each player takes a ball and sees how many touches they can keep going. Then in pairs, working together to keep one ball up between them.

Calm, individual, and genuinely good for touch. It also gives you a couple of minutes to have a quiet word with one or two players without stopping the whole group.
drills.setup: Anywhere with space. One ball per player, then one between two.
coachingPoints: Small, soft touches — don't kick it, cushion it
Laces or thigh, keep the ankle locked
Beat your own score, not anyone else's
In pairs, tell your partner before you play it to them
progressions: Alternate feet on every touch
Add a knee or head touch into the sequence
In pairs, one touch each before it goes back
regressions: Allow a bounce between touches
Catch after every two touches, then restart

drills.name: Tag and Rescue
drills.summary: A tag game where a caught player freezes until a team-mate leaps over to free them.
drills.description:
Everyone moves around the grid. Two or three taggers try to touch the others on the shoulder or back. Anyone tagged crouches down and stays there until a team-mate runs over and leap-frogs them, which puts them straight back in.

Two of the runners carry a ball in their hands, and whoever is holding one cannot be tagged. That turns it from a running game into a **looking** game — the ball is protection, so players have to spot who is about to get caught and throw it to them.

Run it in bursts of two or three minutes and swap the taggers each time.
drills.setup: A 20x20 yard grid. Two balls, carried in the hands to start with. Pick two or three taggers for a group of ten.
coachingPoints: Look for the player in trouble, not just the space in front of you
Shout before you throw so they know it is coming
Taggers: pick one target and commit rather than drifting between two
Free a team-mate as soon as you see them down — nobody stays out long
progressions: Pass the ball with your feet instead of throwing it
Add a third tagger
Shrink the grid so there is less space to run into
regressions: Make the grid bigger
Add a third protecting ball

diagram.caption: Two balls in play; holding one makes you safe.

drills.name: Two-Goal 1v1
drills.summary: Receive under pressure, turn out, and pick which of two goals to attack.
drills.description:
A long, narrow area with a goal and a keeper at each end. Two queues work at the same time from opposite sides.

A player passes in to a receiver standing by the middle cone, then immediately closes them down. The receiver has to take a positive first touch away from the pressure and then decide which goal to go at. If the defender wins it, they attack the other goal.

The defender becomes the next attacker, the attacker rejoins the queue, and it runs continuously.
drills.setup: About 30 x 15 yards, a goal and keeper at each end, a cone in the middle to receive beside. Split the group into two queues on opposite touchlines.
coachingPoints: First touch decides the whole thing — take it away from the presser, not under your feet
Know which goal is emptier before the ball reaches you
Passer: pass it firmly, then press properly — a soft press teaches nothing
Defender: if you win it, go immediately; the other goal is unguarded for about two seconds
progressions: The attacker must beat the defender twice — turn back and score in the other goal
Presser starts a yard closer, so there is less time on the first touch
regressions: Widen the area so the receiver has more room to turn
Presser starts passive and only becomes live after the first touch

diagram.caption: Receive by the middle cone, then attack either goal.

drills.name: Target Player Game
drills.summary: Small-sided game where finding the target player in the end zone doubles the goal.
drills.description:
A game with a goal and keeper at each end and a marked end zone in front of each goal. One player from each team starts as the target inside the opposition end zone; everyone else plays a three-a-side in the middle.

A goal scored straight from the middle is worth one. A goal that goes through the target player is worth two — either the target turns and finishes, or the player who fed them runs in, gets it back and finishes first time.

The doubled score does the coaching for you. Nobody has to be told to look forward.
drills.setup: Roughly 40 x 25 yards, goals and keepers at each end, an end zone about 5 yards deep at each end. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Can you play forward? Look there first, sideways second
Target: come off the back defender so the pass has somewhere to arrive
Feed the target and keep running — the return is where the goal comes from
Weight it so they can turn, not so they have to control it twice
progressions: Allow one defender into the end zone to mark the target
Passes into the target must be first time
regressions: Make the middle area bigger
Two targets per team so there is always one free

diagram.caption: Score through the target in the end zone and it counts double.

drills.name: Crossing the Grid
drills.summary: Ball each, travel across the grid using a different move every time.
drills.description:
Split a square down the middle so there are two halves. Every player has a ball. They travel across one half in one direction, working a move as they go, then come back across the other half in the opposite direction.

Because everyone is moving through the same space at once, it is busy — players have to keep their heads up and use both feet without being told to.

You can start it with no balls at all, just moving across in as many different ways as they can find, then add the ball once they are warm.
drills.setup: A 20x20 yard square split into two halves. One ball per player.
coachingPoints: Both feet, every crossing
Look up between touches — the traffic is the point
Change the move each time rather than repeating your favourite
Small touches in the crowd, longer ones when it opens up
progressions: Put a defender in each half to evade
Call a specific move for each crossing
Race: how many clean crossings in ninety seconds
regressions: No ball at all — just movement patterns across the grid
Bigger halves so there is less traffic

diagram.caption: Across one half, back through the other.

drills.name: Outside-In Possession
drills.summary: Four players on the edge with a ball each, four inside working to receive.
drills.description:
Four players stand around the outside of a square, each with a ball. Four more work inside without one.

An inside player moves to show for a ball, receives from whichever outside player they have made an angle with, and plays it back out to a **different** outside player. Then they move and do it again.

Everybody is busy at once — there is no queue, and no waiting for one ball to come round. Insist on the ball going back out to a different player, otherwise they stop scanning and just bounce it back where it came from.
drills.setup: A 20x20 yard square. Four players on the edges with a ball each, four inside. Swap over every two minutes.
coachingPoints: Check away before you come to show — nobody receives standing still
Look over your shoulder before it arrives so you already know where it is going
Open your body so both sides of the square are available
Play it out to someone different from the one who fed you
progressions: Add a defender inside to press whoever is receiving
Two touches maximum inside
Inside players must turn and play out the far side
regressions: Outside players throw and the inside player heads or volleys back
Shrink to three outside and two inside so the picture is simpler

diagram.caption: Receive from one side, play out to a different one.

drills.name: Forward Only
drills.summary: A normal small-sided game with one rule: you cannot pass backwards.
drills.description:
Play a straight small-sided game with goals and keepers, with one condition — every pass must go forwards or square. No backwards passes at all.

It sounds restrictive and it is, deliberately. Players who normally solve everything by turning and passing back have to find another answer, which usually means moving *before* the ball arrives so there is a forward option to hit.

Expect it to be scrappy for a few minutes. Let that happen. The bit worth waiting for is when they start running past the ball instead of standing still asking for it.
drills.setup: A 40 x 30 pitch, goal and keeper at each end, bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Get ahead of the ball early — if nobody is forward there is no pass
Carry it forward yourself when the pass is not on
Angles, not straight lines: give them something to hit past the defender
Receiving player, open up so forward is the first thing you can see
progressions: The first touch must also go forwards
Backwards passing allowed in your own half only
regressions: Square passes count as forwards
Free play in your own half, forward-only in the attacking half

diagram.caption: Every pass forwards or square — never back.

drills.name: Through, Around or Over
drills.summary: Switch the ball end to end by playing through, around, or over a blocked middle.
drills.description:
Target players stand in a gate at each end of a rectangle. Four players work inside, with two mannequins or poles standing in as a midfield they cannot pass through easily.

The job is to get the ball from one target to the other. There are only three ways to do it: **through** the gap between the obstacles, **around** the outside, or **over** the top. Whoever plays the successful pass into the target swaps in and becomes the new target.

Naming the three routes out loud is what makes this stick. Players start announcing which one they are going for, which means they are choosing rather than hoping.
drills.setup: A rectangle sized to the group — long enough that "over" is a real option. Two poles or mannequins across the middle, a gate at each end with a target player inside.
coachingPoints: Look at the obstacle before you look at the target — the route decides the pass
Through needs weight and accuracy; over needs height and a soft landing
Move the ball sideways first to change the angle, then go
Target: show on the side that opens the next pass
progressions: Count how many successful switches in ninety seconds and beat it
Add a live defender who can block the through-ball
Each route scores differently: through 3, around 1, over 2
regressions: Take the mannequins out and just switch end to end
Shorten the rectangle so the passes are shorter

diagram.caption: Three routes end to end: through, around, over.

drills.name: Corner Gates Possession
drills.summary: Four v four, scoring by finding a target player standing in a corner gate.
drills.description:
A square with a gate marked in two opposite corners, each holding a target player. Inside is a four-a-side.

The team in possession scores by playing into either of their target players. Whoever plays that pass swaps places with the target, and possession turns over to the other team straight away.

Two corners rather than one end means there is always a switch available, so the team defending cannot just squeeze one side. It also means the answer is usually to move the ball across before going forward.
drills.setup: A 25x25 yard square. A cone gate in two opposite corners with a target player inside each. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: If one corner is crowded, the other one is free — switch it
Target: move within your gate to open a line
Play the pass you can see now, not the one you want in two seconds
Defending team: protect the corners first, chase the ball second
progressions: Score different points depending on how the target was found
Two touches maximum
Add a floating player who always plays for whoever has the ball
regressions: Bigger square
Widen the gates so the target is easier to find

diagram.caption: Two corner gates — if one is shut, switch to the other.

drills.name: Name Your Route
drills.summary: A game where you have to say how you got through: around, over, or straight through.
drills.description:
A normal game with goals at each end, and a box marked out across the middle of the pitch. The attacking team has to get past that box one of three ways: **through** it, **around** the outside of it, or **over** the top.

When a team scores, they have to shout which route they used for the goal to count. Anyone who cannot say gets nothing.

That sounds like a gimmick and it partly is, but it makes them notice the decision they just made. After a few goals you hear players calling the route *before* they play the pass, which is the whole point.
drills.setup: A 40 x 30 pitch with goals at each end. Mark a box across the middle third with cones or poles. Even teams, bibs for one side.
coachingPoints: Decide the route before you receive, not after
Around is safest, through is quickest, over is the one nobody expects
If they block one route, the other two open up — look again
Say it out loud; if you cannot name it, you did not choose it
progressions: Different points per route so the harder ones are worth more
First team to score using all three routes wins
regressions: Two floating players to create an overload
Remove the shouting and just play through, around and over freely

diagram.caption: Past the middle box one of three ways — and name it.

drills.name: Raid the Zone
drills.summary: Two teams raid each other’s end zone to steal balls and carry them home.
drills.description:
Two teams, an end zone each, and a pile of balls in every zone. On the call, players run into the opposition zone, grab a ball and dribble it back to their own.

Anyone tagged on the way has to leave the ball and run back to their own zone before setting off again. No tackling — a touch on the back or shoulder is enough.

The good bit is that everyone is attacking and defending at once. Players work out for themselves that if the whole team raids, their own zone is wide open.
drills.setup: At least 30 x 20 yards with a marked zone at each end. Six to eight balls in each zone to start.
coachingPoints: Look before you set off — go where the defenders are not
Big touches in the open, small ones near a defender
Somebody has to stay home; sort that out between you
Tagged? Reset quickly rather than arguing about it
progressions: Make the area bigger so the carry is longer
Taggers can tackle, not just touch
Only the ball in your hands counts — no dribbling
regressions: Fewer players so there is more space
Fixed raiders and fixed defenders rather than everyone doing both

diagram.caption: Steal a ball, carry it home, avoid the tag.

drills.name: Corner Relay
drills.summary: Teams race a ball around four corner boxes, handing over at each one.
drills.description:
Mark a box in each corner of a square. Two teams each put a player in every box, and each team starts with one ball.

The first player runs the ball into the next box, leaves it for the team-mate waiting there, and stays. That player takes it on to the next box. One team goes clockwise, the other anticlockwise, so they pass each other in the middle.

Count laps for a set time. It is a running-with-the-ball drill dressed up as a race, which is the only reason players will do that many repetitions of it.
drills.setup: About 30 x 20 yards with a small box coned off in each corner. One ball per team, players spread one to a box.
coachingPoints: Big touches — cover ground, do not dribble it in tiny steps
Head up: the other team is coming the other way
Leave the ball still for the next player, do not fire it at them
Take the first touch into the direction you are already going
progressions: Bigger area so the carries are longer
Change the route — diagonal across, then round the edge
Two balls per team at once
regressions: Smaller area
Bigger corner boxes so the receiving touch is easier

diagram.caption: One team clockwise, one anticlockwise.

drills.name: Free in the Channel
drills.summary: A game with wide channels where anyone who enters gets to run unopposed.
drills.description:
A normal small-sided game, with a narrow channel marked down each touchline. Anyone who receives or carries the ball into a channel cannot be tackled — they get to run with it and then decide: cross, cut back, come inside, or shoot.

Goals scored straight from a channel count treble; assists from one count double.

The scoring is doing the coaching. Players who normally never look up start scanning for the channel as an escape from pressure, and the ones who live out there learn there is a decision at the end of the run, not just a sprint.
drills.setup: A 40 x 30 pitch, goals and keepers. Mark a channel 3 to 4 yards wide down each side. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: The channel is an escape from pressure — use it when you are stuck, not by default
Laces, big touches, cover ground while nobody can touch you
Head up while you run: the decision matters more than the run
Cut-backs beat high crosses more often than players expect
progressions: Let one defender follow you in, so it becomes a 1v1
Time limit in the channel or the ball turns over
regressions: Wider channels
Allow players to carry it the full length of the pitch

diagram.caption: In the channel, nobody can touch you.

drills.name: Share the Ball
drills.summary: Everyone moving, four balls between the group, pass to anyone who shows for it.
drills.description:
The whole group moves around the area. Four of them start with a ball. Anyone without one gets themselves into a position to receive; anyone with one looks to give it away.

No teams, no direction, no queues — the only rule is that you should not be standing still whether you have the ball or not.

It looks like nothing much and it is the most reliable warm-up I know for getting heads up. Because four balls are moving at once, players cannot switch off waiting for their turn.
drills.setup: An area sized to the group. Four balls between eight to twelve players. Bibs optional.
coachingPoints: Move to a place where a pass can actually reach you
Call for it — name, not just a shout
Look before it arrives so you know your next one
Pass and go somewhere new; do not admire it
progressions: Pass only to your own colour
Count team passes in thirty seconds and beat it
Add two defenders trying to win a ball
regressions: More balls
Bigger area

diagram.caption: Four balls moving, nobody standing still.

drills.name: Crossbar Challenge
drills.summary: Strike a moving ball at the crossbar from a central feed.
drills.description:
A goal at each end and a small central area. Half the group stand at the corners with a supply of balls; the rest wait in the middle.

A corner player rolls one into a middle player, who strikes it first time — or with one touch to set — trying to hit the crossbar. Swap the groups over after a few minutes.

Aiming at the bar rather than the goal is the whole trick: it stops players scooping the ball over and forces them to get their head and knee over it. Keep score if you want, but the technique is the point.
drills.setup: A goal at each end with a coned area in the middle. Several balls at each corner. Split into two groups.
coachingPoints: Non-kicking foot alongside the ball, not behind it
Head still and over the ball to keep it down
Strike through the middle of it with the laces
Follow through towards the target rather than stopping the foot
progressions: Keep score per team
Everyone has a ball and rolls it out of their own feet before striking
regressions: Shorten the distance
Strike a stationary ball first

diagram.caption: Fed from the corner, struck at the bar.

drills.name: Balls on Cones
drills.summary: A game where knocking a ball off a cone scores, but a clean net finish scores double.
drills.description:
A normal small-sided game with no keepers. Balance two balls on cones just inside each post.

Knock one of those off and you score one. Score properly, into the net without it bouncing first, and you get two.

With no keeper, the targets give a smaller, more precise thing to aim at than an empty net, and the double for a clean finish stops players just poking it along the floor at the cones. Play to a set score rather than a set time.
drills.setup: Goals at each end, no keepers. Two balls balanced on cones inside each set of posts. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Pick your target before you shoot, not while you shoot
A clean strike is worth twice as much — take the extra half-second
Get a shot away early; the targets do not move but the defenders do
Follow it in — knocked-off balls create scrambles
progressions: Double points for scoring from your own half
A time or passing limit before a shot must be taken
regressions: Smaller pitch so shots come from closer
Three balls per goal

diagram.caption: Knock a ball off for one, a clean finish for two.

drills.name: Thirty-Second Duel
drills.summary: Paired 1v1 where whoever has the ball when the whistle goes wins the point.
drills.description:
Everyone is paired with an opponent inside one area. Every pair has a ball, and one player starts with it.

For thirty seconds the two of them fight over it. Whoever has it when the whistle goes wins a point for their team. If it goes out, the other player restarts with it.

Because every pair is going at once it is genuinely chaotic, which is the point — players have to shield the ball while other duels crash past them. Swap who starts with the ball each round and shorten the time as they get better at it.
drills.setup: One area big enough for all the pairs, sized down as the group improves. One ball per pair, bibs to tell the teams apart.
coachingPoints: Body between the defender and the ball, always
Use your arm to feel where they are without pushing
Move it — a shielded ball that never travels gets won eventually
Defender: be patient, wait for the heavy touch rather than lunging
progressions: Score by taking the ball into your own team’s half
Shrink the area
Cut it to twenty seconds
regressions: Bigger area
Longer rounds so there is time to recover from a mistake

diagram.caption: Every pair fighting for their own ball at once.

drills.name: Attack Then Defend
drills.summary: Continuous 1v1 to two mini goals where the attacker becomes the next defender.
drills.description:
Two mini goals at one end, two queues at the other. One player goes out to defend them.

The first attacker dribbles at the defender and tries to score in either goal. The moment that attack finishes — scored or not — the attacker turns and becomes the defender against the next player coming out.

That switch is the whole exercise. Players spend half a second going from wanting the ball to wanting to win it back, which is the transition moment that decides most games at this age.
drills.setup: Two mini goals at one end with a scoring line in front of them. Two queues of players at the other end, a ball each.
coachingPoints: Attackers: run at them, make them decide which goal to protect
Change of pace beats a stepover on its own
The second it turns over, get set — do not stand there disappointed
Defender: side-on, show them to one goal and stay patient
progressions: Bigger goals with keepers
Defender who wins it scores by dribbling into a middle square
regressions: Smaller area so the transition is shorter
Give the attacker a head start

diagram.caption: Attack, then immediately defend the next one.

drills.name: Win It and Go
drills.summary: Score in the same possession you won the ball and it counts double.
drills.description:
A normal game with one scoring rule: if a team wins the ball back and scores before losing it again, the goal is worth two. If the ball goes out first and comes back in from a throw or a corner, it is only worth one.

It rewards the two or three seconds straight after a turnover, which is when defences are least organised and when almost nobody at youth level is looking up.

Expect them to over-commit at first and get caught. That is fine — it is the same lesson from the other side.
drills.setup: Pitch sized to the group, goals and keepers at each end, bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: The second you win it, look forward before you look sideways
Nearest player to the ball presses; everyone else gets ahead of it
Do not slow down to take a nice touch — go
If they win it off you, sprint back straight away rather than protesting
progressions: Score within three seconds of winning it and it is worth five
Extra points for a first-time finish
regressions: Smaller pitch so the ball can be won back more easily
Count any goal after a turnover, no time pressure

diagram.caption: Win it and score before losing it: double.

drills.name: Guard the Gates
drills.summary: Escapers try to run through gates that guards are defending.
drills.description:
Mark two gates along each side of the area, each with a guard standing in it. Four escapers start in the middle.

On the call the escapers try to run through any gate without being tagged. Through cleanly is a point to them; a tag is a point to the guard.

It is a defending exercise disguised as a chase. Guards learn very quickly that standing square in the middle of the gate gets them beaten, and that a side-on stance covering one side lets them react to either.
drills.setup: An area sized to the group with two gates on each side. One guard per gate, four escapers in the middle.
coachingPoints: Guards: side-on, small steps, never crossing your feet
Show them one side and cover the other
Escapers: change direction late; the first move should be a lie
Do not commit until they do
progressions: Escapers dribble a ball through the gate
Wider gates so guards have more to cover
More escapers at once
regressions: Narrower gates
Smaller playing area

diagram.caption: Through a gate scores; a tag scores for the guard.

drills.name: Line Stealers
drills.summary: Pairs pass across a line while a stealer, stuck on that line, tries to intercept.
drills.description:
Split the area into channels with a line running across the middle. Pairs face each other across the channels with a ball, passing back and forth — a point for each clean pass.

One or two stealers work along the middle line and cannot leave it. They try to intercept. If a stealer wins one, they dribble it past the player who gave it away and over the end line; if they make it, they swap roles with that player.

Because the stealer is restricted to the line, the passers can beat them by timing rather than power, which is a more useful thing to learn than just hitting it harder.
drills.setup: A 20 x 20 area split into channels, with a line across the middle. Pairs facing across, one ball each, one or two stealers on the line.
coachingPoints: Look at the stealer, not just your partner — pass when they have committed elsewhere
Firm and along the floor; a floated pass gives them time
Stealer: watch the hips, not the ball
Move along your line rather than lunging across it
progressions: Wider channels so the stealer covers more ground
Allow passes in the air
Add a second stealer
regressions: Narrower channels
Passers may take as many touches as they like

diagram.caption: The stealer is stuck on the middle line.

drills.name: Locked-In Quarters
drills.summary: A game split into quarters with one player from each team locked into each.
drills.description:
Divide the pitch into four quarters with a line down the middle and one across. One player from each team is locked into each quarter — they cannot leave it.

Normal rules otherwise, goals and keepers at both ends. Every quarter is its own permanent 1v1, so the game becomes four private battles that happen to add up to a match.

It is a good way to give a player who hides in games nowhere to hide, and a good way to stop one strong player covering every blade of grass. Rotate who is paired with whom so it does not become a mismatch all session.
drills.setup: A 30 x 20 pitch marked into four quarters, goals and keepers at each end. Eight outfield players, one pair per quarter.
coachingPoints: Your quarter is yours — win it and the team wins
Get across your opponent before the pass arrives, not after
Show for it every time the ball is on your side
Defending: anticipate the pass into your quarter and step on it
progressions: Let players move between quarters to create overloads
Bigger pitch so the duels cover more ground
regressions: Smaller pitch
Add touch limits so the ball moves faster

diagram.caption: Four permanent 1v1s inside one game.

drills.name: Wave Attack
drills.summary: A 2v1 that grows to 3v2, then 4v3, adding a player each time the ball goes dead.
drills.description:
Two teams either side of a halfway line, goals and keepers at both ends. It starts as a 2v1 attacking one goal.

As soon as that attack ends — goal, save or out — one attacker and one defender join in, making it 3v2. Then 4v3, and so on until everyone is on. If the defending team wins it, they attack the other goal.

Every wave gives the attackers a spare player, so there is always a right answer available. What changes is how quickly they find it as the numbers and the noise go up.
drills.setup: A pitch split in half with a goal and keeper at each end, teams waiting on their own touchline. Balls with the coach.
coachingPoints: Find the spare player — there is always one
Attack quickly before the extra defender arrives
Width first, then attack the gap it opens
Defenders: delay, do not dive in when you are outnumbered
progressions: Attackers can only score after creating an overload in one half
Time limit on each wave
regressions: Add two attackers per wave and one defender
Start at 3v1 so the first wave is easier

diagram.caption: Each wave adds one attacker and one defender.

drills.name: Half-Court 2v2
drills.summary: Two 2v2 games running at once, one in each half, with two balls in play.
drills.description:
Split the pitch in half. Each team puts two players in each half, so there is a 2v2 going on at both ends at the same time — with two balls in play.

Attackers start from the halfway line. Score and you restart. If the defenders win it, all they have to do is stop the ball on the halfway line, and then the roles swap.

Two games at once means twice the repetitions and no waiting. It also means it is loud and looks like chaos from the touchline; that is normal.
drills.setup: An area with a goal and keeper at each end, split across the middle. Two players from each team in each half. Two balls.
coachingPoints: One goes, one supports — never both at the ball
Attack before the second defender gets across
Defenders: stopping it on the line is a win, you do not have to score
Play your own game; ignore the one behind you
progressions: Players may cross into either half as long as one team-mate stays
Make it 3v2 in one half
regressions: One ball at a time
Bigger halves so there is more room to work

diagram.caption: Two 2v2s, two balls, at once.

drills.name: Knockout Goals
drills.summary: Score, and one of the opposition has to sit out for thirty seconds.
drills.description:
A normal game, but every goal sends one opposition player off for thirty seconds. They come straight back if their team scores in the meantime.

A team that scores twice quickly is suddenly two players up, which snowballs — and knocking out the whole opposition at once wins it outright.

It is unashamedly a fun game, and it teaches something real: when you are a player down you have to be more compact, and when you are a player up you have to move the ball rather than force it.
drills.setup: Pitch and goals sized to the group, keepers optional. Bibs for one team. Somebody needs to keep the thirty seconds.
coachingPoints: A player up: move the ball, do not force it — the space will come
A player down: get compact and make them play round you
Score again quickly to get your team-mate back
Keep playing while they are counting — restarts are fast
progressions: Longer time off the pitch
A knocked-out player must run round their own goal before returning
regressions: Shorter time off
Only the first goal in each spell knocks anyone out

diagram.caption: Each goal sends an opponent off for thirty seconds.

drills.name: In Line With Your Partner
drills.summary: Ball mastery across a square, staying level with a partner on the far side.
drills.description:
Pairs face each other across a square, a ball each. Both set off at the same time, working the same move — sole rolls, toe taps, whatever you have been showing them — and the job is to arrive at the other side **level with each other**.

That one condition is what makes it more than a ball-mastery drill. To stay level you have to keep glancing up to find your partner, which is exactly the scanning habit you want and exactly the thing players stop doing the moment they concentrate on their feet.

Count touches across if you want a competitive edge.
drills.setup: A 20x20 square, pairs facing each other from opposite sides, one ball per player.
coachingPoints: Look up to find your partner, then back down — not one long stare at the ball
Both feet on every crossing
Match their speed; arriving first is not the win
Keep the touches small enough that a glance up does not cost you the ball
progressions: Change the move each crossing
Add a pass at the far side, then that player crosses
More pairs so there is traffic to navigate
regressions: Cross at your own pace, ignore staying level
Fewer pairs in the square

diagram.caption: Arrive at the far side level with your partner.

drills.name: Two Ways Across
drills.summary: Two teams working at right angles in the same square, each with their own target players.
drills.description:
One square, two teams, and each is trying to move the ball across it in a **different direction** — one team works left to right, the other top to bottom. Each has two target players waiting on their own pair of sides.

Start unopposed with a ball each so they get used to the pattern and the traffic. Then take it down to one ball and let them compete: transfer target to target for a point, and the other team tries to win it and go their own way.

The crossing lines are the whole idea. Players cannot just look up one channel; there is always someone travelling across their path.
drills.setup: A 20x20 grid. Two players from each team inside, two on their own opposite sides as targets. Bibs to tell the teams apart.
coachingPoints: Scan across the square, not just up your own line
Open your body so both of your targets are available
Move the defender before you play it, not after
Target players: shift along your side to open the angle
progressions: One ball only and play the two teams against each other
Target players may dribble in, with a team-mate taking their place
Targets can be tackled too
regressions: Both teams have a ball and work unopposed
Bigger grid

diagram.caption: One team across, one team up and down.

drills.name: Retreat or Press
drills.summary: From a goal kick the opposition must retreat — then choose whether to press or hold.
drills.description:
A small-sided game with keepers. Whenever a team has a goal kick, the other team has to drop into their own half. Break that and it is a free kick to the team in possession.

Once the first pass is played, the defending team chooses: come and press, or stay and stay compact. That choice is the interesting bit — it is a decision, not a rule, and different players will read it differently.

It gives the team building out a genuine chance to play rather than being swarmed on the six-yard line, without pretending pressing does not exist.
drills.setup: A 40 x 20 area, goals and keepers at each end, marked halfway line. Three or four a side.
coachingPoints: Get wide and deep the moment the keeper has it
Keeper is a player — use them to switch
Defenders: decide together, half of you pressing is worse than neither
If the first pass is not on, go back and round — do not force it
progressions: No retreat line at all — press from wherever you like
Attacking team must make a set number of passes before crossing halfway
regressions: Defenders must stay in their half until the ball crosses the line
Add a neutral player for the team building out

diagram.caption: They retreat for the goal kick, then choose.

drills.name: Stop It on a Cone
drills.summary: A 1v1 inside a small box where you score by stopping the ball on any of four cones.
drills.description:
Split a square into a grid of small boxes and put a 1v1 in each, with a cone in every corner of the box and a ball between the two.

You score by stopping the ball dead on top of one of the four cones. Once you have scored you cannot use that same cone again straight away, so the attacker has to change direction rather than working one favourite move over and over.

Winners move up a box, losers move down. That ladder is what keeps the effort up for the full minute.
drills.setup: A 25x25 area split into a 3x3 grid of boxes. Four cones in each box, one ball per pair. Play one-minute rounds.
coachingPoints: Attack the cone they are furthest from
Change of pace, then change of direction — in that order
Defender: side-on, deny the nearest cone and show them across
Stopping it properly counts — a scuffed touch off the cone is nothing
progressions: Players are not fixed to a box and may go anywhere
Start with the defender passing in and the attacker naming their target cone
regressions: No ball at all — the defender pulls a bib from the attacker’s shorts
Bigger boxes

diagram.caption: Stop the ball on a cone to score.

drills.name: Diagonal Goals 1v1
drills.summary: Two 1v1 pitches side by side with the goals diagonally opposite each other.
drills.description:
Split a rectangle into two long pitches with a goal at one end of each — but put them **diagonally opposite**, so the goal you attack and the goal you defend are at opposite corners of the whole area.

One defender works on each pitch. An attacker takes them on and tries to score. If the defender wins it, they can go and score in the goal at their own end.

The diagonal placement means winning the ball is genuinely worth something rather than just clearing it, and it keeps both pitches running at once so nobody is standing around.
drills.setup: A 40 x 20 area split into two 20 x 10 pitches. One goal per pitch, diagonally opposite. A defender on each, attackers queueing at the far ends.
coachingPoints: Defender: deny first, delay second — do not lunge
Show them away from your goal and towards the touchline
Attacker: run at them, do not slow down and invite the tackle
Win it and go straight away — the other goal is a long way from them
progressions: Play it as a 2v2 on each pitch
Add a keeper in each goal
regressions: Defenders press but cannot tackle
Work in pairs, attacking one goal then the other

diagram.caption: Goals diagonally opposite — winning it is worth something.

drills.name: Ladder Zones 2v2
drills.summary: Three 2v2 pitches side by side, winners move up, losers move down.
drills.description:
Split a square into three narrow pitches, each with a goal at both ends — six goals in total. A 2v2 on each, and you have to get into the final third of your pitch before you can score.

Short games, then winners move up a pitch and losers move down. The ladder sorts itself out within a few rounds and everyone ends up playing someone their own level, which is worth more than any coaching point.

Defending in pairs is the thing to watch. In a narrow pitch two defenders who stay connected are almost impossible to get past; two who both chase the ball get opened up every time.
drills.setup: A 25x25 area split into three pitches, a goal at both ends of each. Two v two on each pitch. Play three-minute games.
coachingPoints: One presses, one covers — never both at the ball
Talk to each other; you cannot defend as a pair in silence
If the ball goes out, get set before it comes back in
Attacking: get into the final third first, then look for the finish
progressions: When a team concedes, one of them must run and touch the far goal first — a temporary 2v1
Winners move up two pitches instead of one
regressions: Winning the ball back and keeping it counts as a goal
Wider pitches

diagram.caption: Three pitches, winners move up.

drills.name: Pairs Through the Gates
drills.summary: Pairs run through defended gates together, arriving at the same time.
drills.description:
A square with two gates in each corner. One group are taggers, the other work in pairs.

The pairs try to get through either of the two gates at the far end — **both of them, at the same time**. One arriving alone does not count. That forces them to talk, time it, and split the taggers between them rather than both running at the same gap.

Swap the groups over regularly. It is a warm-up but it is quietly teaching a two-player attacking pattern.
drills.setup: A 20x20 square with two cone gates in each corner. Split into taggers and pairs of attackers.
coachingPoints: Split them — if you both run at one gate, one of you gets caught
Call it early so your partner knows which gate you are going for
Vary who leads; the tagger will follow the first runner
Taggers: stay between the two of them for as long as you can
progressions: Attackers may cross the halfway line and check back through their own gates
Add a ball for the pair to pass between them
regressions: Play it as a 1v1 instead of pairs
Wider gates

diagram.caption: Both of you through, at the same time.

drills.name: Halfway There
drills.summary: Two v two locked in each half — dribble into the other half to score.
drills.description:
Split a pitch in two, with a goal and keeper at each end and a 2v2 in each half. Players are locked into their own half, with one exception: the player who carries the ball over the line.

The keeper starts it with their own attackers. To score, one of them has to **dribble** into the far half and finish, which means beating someone and then dealing with what is waiting.

Because only the ball-carrier can cross, it is genuinely a 1v2 the moment they arrive. That sounds unfair and is the point — they learn to pick the right moment rather than setting off every time.
drills.setup: A pitch split into halves, goal and keeper at each end. Two from each team in each half. Bibs.
coachingPoints: Pick your moment — go when they are square or flat-footed
Both feet: a defender only has to cover one side if you only use one
Once you are over, go straight at goal; the cover is coming
Defending pair: force them wide, never let them come inside on their strong foot
progressions: Open it up into a free game where you just have to get into the opposite half to score
A team-mate may follow the carrier across
regressions: Players may move anywhere
Everyone has a ball and simply has to get from one side to the other

diagram.caption: Only the ball-carrier may cross the line.

drills.name: Gate and Strike
drills.summary: Push the ball through a gate with one touch, then finish with the next.
drills.description:
Two lines of players, each with a ball, and a cone gate a few yards in front of each. A goal at each end.

One touch to push the ball through the gate, the next one to strike at goal. Two players go at once — one line working their right foot, the other their left — then they swap lines so everybody does both.

The gate is doing something specific: it forces a proper first touch out of the feet instead of the shuffling-and-poking that happens when players shoot from a static ball.
drills.setup: About 30 x 20 with a goal at each end, keepers optional. A cone gate a few yards in front of each line.
coachingPoints: First touch through the gate and into your stride, not sideways
Strike it while it is still rolling
Non-kicking foot beside the ball; head over it
Aim for the far post — a keeper covers the near one first
progressions: Start with the ball in your hands and strike it on the half volley
Pair up: one carries it wide and cuts it back for the other to finish first time
regressions: Move everything closer to goal
No keepers to start with

diagram.caption: One touch through the gate, one at goal.

drills.name: Chip or Go Round
drills.summary: One-on-one with a keeper who sets the ball back — chip them or take it round.
drills.description:
Two lines either side of the area, a goal at each end, and one player in the middle acting as the keeper for both.
